• Other names: African payal, Butterfly fern, Eared watermoss
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Difficulty: Easy to medium
  • Lighting: moderate to high
  • Substrate: any
  • Growth rate: moderate to fast
  • Placement: floating
  • Fertilizers: recommended
  • CO2: not needed
  • Propagation: vegetatively through fragmentation or by splitting
  • Colour: green

Salvinia auriculata is indigenous to tropical America, presently dominant in Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, El Salvador, Honduras, Mexico, Panama, Paraguay, Peru and Venezuela.

This species has been introduced and can be found naturalized in other parts of the world as an ornamental plant. It is listed as an invasive species in countries like Cuba, Dominican Republic, Taiwan, Zambia and Zimbabwe.

This free-floating fern inhabits still and slow-moving waters ranging from lakes, ponds, rivers, marshes, swamps, ditches, reservoirs and rice fields.

The plant is highly competitive. It can displace native plants and animals, grows rapidly, and is capable of blocking canals and waterways. It thrives best in nutrient-rich warm water and tolerates mild temperate conditions, occasional frost and low salinity levels.

In nature, this plant grows in open ponds, lakes, swamps, etc. with very little shade.

Salvinia auriculata can be kept in tanks of varying sizes and depths since it floats on the water surface. Under optimal conditions it grows very fast and tends to take up a lot of space; even a single plant can cover a 50 cm tank in a fairly short time. A tank of at least 40 litres is recommended.

Care requirements are minimal, but some tips help achieve the best growth.

  • Prune constantly when it overgrows, especially when it covers the surface. Remove some foliage but leave a substantial amount to keep growing and spreading lateral shoots.
  • The plant can cast too much shade. When light does not reach plants at lower levels, their growth is hampered and they may become stunted.
  • When the surface is overcrowded, scoop out some shoots with a skimmer or net, and pick out sick or damaged leaves at the same time.
  • Dispose of collected leaves, preferably sealed in a plastic bag, to prevent them entering local waterways.
  • Watch the colour of the shoots: foliage loses its vibrant colour and may turn yellow when nutrients are lacking. Add fertilizers with essential nutrients in the right doses.
  • Protect the plants from condensation drips, which make them rot. Tilt the tank lid slightly so droplets run down the slope back into the tank rather than onto the leaves.
  • Do partial water changes of about 20–25% every two weeks with clean freshwater. Reduce water flow and provide slow currents.

Planting and propagation

The plant floats flat on the water surface. Just spread the finely divided portions on the water and let them float and branch out.

  • Split and properly disinfect newly purchased plants.
  • Spread the portions uniformly on the water surface. Do not let the plants cover the whole surface; about one-third is fine since they will branch out and spread further.

It propagates vegetatively through fragmentation, i.e. the continuous branching and breaking away of lateral and terminal shoots. Partial death of the plant often stimulates dormant buds to develop, and each node has up to 5 dormant buds. Usually, older stems detach from these nodes as more buds develop. Alternatively, you can split the branches of existing plants to create new ones.

Problems

  • Overgrowth: it may overrun the tank if left unattended and shade plants at the bottom. Prune and discard the dense mass from time to time.
  • Oxygen depletion: without aeration or water flow that disturbs the surface, do not let it form a thick layer for long. It can reduce gas exchange and deplete oxygen in the water, potentially suffocating fish or shrimp.
  • Leaf rot: caused by condensation drips falling on the floating leaves. Limit contact of leaves with droplets, or they may die and ruin water quality as they rot.
  • Discoloration: a sign of poor health, mostly caused by lack of nutrients. Regular fertilizing replenishes nutrients and gives deep green colour and robust growth.

Temperature: the ideal range is 22–26 °C. The warmer the water, the faster the plant grows and the larger its leaves become.

pH: it can grow in a relatively wide range, but the optimal pH is 6.0–8.0.

Hardness: Salvinia auriculata does not care much about hardness and tolerates soft or hard water. For optimal growth, keep hardness at 3–18 GH.

Water flow: in nature it inhabits ponds and shallow streams with slow currents. It often does not survive in fast-moving water (over 0.3 m/s), so still or slow currents are recommended.

Salvinia auriculata thrives in moderate to high light. It needs bright light to grow rapidly and sprout new shoots; under low light its growth declines. Bright light can be provided with an LED light turned on at least 10 hours daily. In nature direct sunlight suits it best, but that is not suitable for tanks housing other plants and animals that may not appreciate direct sunlight or very powerful artificial light, so a balance must be kept.

CO2 injection is not mandatory: the plant does not need CO2 dosing as it takes it from the air.

It draws a great deal of its nutrients from the water, so fertilizers in the water column are much appreciated. Regular fertilizing increases yield and gives a healthier appearance. To increase growth, provide fertilizers (NPK: nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium) or supplements regularly.

If you keep shrimp with this plant, note that high CO2 levels and copper (which most fertilizers contain) are extremely dangerous to shrimp.

Salvinia auriculata belongs to Salviniaceae, a family of heterosporous ferns in the order Salviniales. This family comprises two genera, Azolla and Salvinia. The genus Salvinia is named in honour of Anton Maria Salvini, a 17th-century Italian scientist, and contains 12 known species which are quite similar in morphology.

It is a floating fern with horizontally growing abundant shoots. It can go dormant during unfavourable conditions and resume growth when conditions improve. Unlike true perennials, it does not have a rootstock or rhizome to die back into. Its colour varies from bright green to olive-green.

It features numerous leaves arranged in whorls of three. Two are floating (often 1–3 cm), while one stays submerged. The floating leaves are densely covered with fine protective, egg-beater shaped hairs, and the third leaf in each whorl is modified into a finely divided root-like structure of about 2.5–5 cm.

The plant changes morphology depending on environmental conditions, with primary, secondary and tertiary growth forms. Floating leaves of the primary form are flat, well-spaced, oval with slightly lobed bases. Leaves of the tertiary form are densely crowded and tightly folded upwards along the mid-vein, whereas floating leaves of the secondary form are intermediate between the two.

Salvinia auriculata lacks true roots and depends on the hair-like projections of the submerged leaves to function as roots. The submerged leaves also bear spore-producing structures known as sporocarps.

Sometimes this plant is confused with Salvinia natans, which is practically not used in the aquarium hobby, since it is an annual plant.

Benefits

  • Breeding ground: provides a breeding ground for egg scatterers and dwarf shrimp.
  • Shelter/cover: provides cover and shade for species that prefer low light. Its submerged root-like leaves provide hiding spots for fry and juvenile fish.
  • Light penetration: can filter light for plants that do not need it (for example Java fern, Amazon sword, Marimo moss ball, Anubias), diffusing very bright aquarium lighting.
  • Oxygenation: promotes oxygenation through photosynthesis and also absorbs toxins harmful to aquatic life.
  • Algae control: helps inhibit algae growth by outcompeting algae for the available nutrients.
  • Aesthetics: its dense green foliage makes the aquarium look more natural.
  • Removal of excess nutrients: helps maintain water quality by removing harmful substances such as ammonia, nitrate, nitrite and heavy metals. As it grows rapidly, it needs lots of nutrients.

Tankmates

Salvinia auriculata should be kept with species that thrive in a shaded aquarium.

  • Fish: Corydoras catfish, neon tetras, ember tetras, guppies, mollies, Otocinclus catfish, pygmy Corydoras.
  • Shrimp: cherry shrimp, snowball shrimp, Caridina cf. babaulti, ghost shrimp, Amano shrimp, blue tiger shrimp, blue velvet shrimp, vampire shrimp, bamboo shrimp, cardinal shrimp, red nose shrimp, etc.
  • Freshwater snails: Japanese trapdoor snails, ramshorn snails, nerite snails, Malaysian trumpet snails, black devil snails, Asolene spixi, rabbit snails, etc.

Avoid large, aggressive and plant-eating fish that will quickly tear up the plant, for example goldfish, oscars, rainbowfish, Jack Dempsey and clown loaches.

Buying

Due to its popularity, this floating plant is easily obtainable at local fish stores and online. Alternatively, you can ask nearby hobbyists for a portion. Healthy plants have vibrant green colouration and the shoots should be free of abnormalities.

Quarantine

Quarantine the plant before putting it into your aquarium.

  • The plant can carry parasites, pests such as snails, or even predators (dragonfly and damselfly nymphs, etc.).
  • It could also have been treated with pesticides to remove parasites, snails, etc. These chemicals are extremely poisonous to fish, shrimp and other invertebrates.
